title: Adam and Christ (Romans 5:12–21)
hookLine: where sin increased, grace abounded all the more

cards: Some things you inherit without asking. Your grandmother's nose. Your family's way of going quiet when things get tense.

A house, or a debt. You didn't choose any of it, and it shapes you anyway. In the second half of Romans chapter five, Paul steps way back from Rome and his own day, all the way to the garden in Genesis.
He's thinking about the whole human family and what it has inherited. And he sets two figures side by side, like two ends of a seesaw: the first man, and one more.

teach.b: Paul begins, in the King James Bible: "Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned."
One man, Adam, opened a door, and sin and death came through it into the whole human story.
Then the other end of the seesaw: "For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous." Adam and Christ. One disobeyed, one obeyed.
One brought death, one brings life.

teach.h: NOT AN EVEN SEESAW: MUCH MORE.
teach.b: But Paul keeps insisting it isn't an even seesaw. Again and again he says much more: the gift is not like the fall. Then the line of the day: "But where sin abounded, grace did much more abound."
Paul reaches for a super-word in Greek: grace super-abounded, over-overflowed. However big the mess gets, grace is bigger. Christians understand the Adam side differently.
In the West, following Augustine, Catholics and the churches of the Reformation speak of original sin: every person is born sharing in Adam's fallen state, even in some sense his guilt.
Orthodox Christians usually speak of ancestral sin: we inherit mortality and a wounded nature, but not Adam's personal guilt.
Some scholars trace part of that difference to how one small phrase here was translated into Latin. Either way, Paul's direction is plain. The chapter doesn't end with Adam.
It ends with grace reigning, through Jesus Christ.

how: Christians read Romans 5 when they teach about sin and salvation, and in the Easter Vigil's ancient hymn, the Exsultet, Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran churches sing of Adam's fall and of the grace that came after it.

games.q: you're Paul. you've just said sin and death came into the world through one man. how do you describe what Christ brings?
o: exactly equal: one cancels out the other.
much more: where sin abounded, grace abounded more.
smaller: enough for some, not for all.
games.why: Paul keeps saying much more. the gift is not like the fall: "where sin abounded, grace did much more abound."

practice: Think of a mistake, yours or someone else's, that turned out smaller than what came after it: a fight that ended in a better friendship, a wrong turn that led somewhere good, someone who forgave you more than you expected.
Don't explain it away; just let yourself see that the mistake wasn't the end of the story. If you pray, thank God for that grace, by name.

wordCard.voice: Charis. Paul's Greek word for grace: a gift freely given, which he says super-abounds wherever sin abounds.

orig.note: Greek: grace, favor, a gift freely given. the root of the word Eucharist, thanksgiving.

carryVoice: Your line: grace abounds. On Paul's seesaw, grace is always the heavier side. That's day three hundred seventeen.
